citation.title: Deep learning aided topology optimization of phononic crystals
citation.authors: Paweł Kudela, Abdalraheem Ijjeh, Maciej Radzieński, Marco Miniaci, Nicola Pugno, Wiesław Ostachowicz
citation.venue: Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing 200 (2023) 110636 (available online 30 July 2023; CC BY 4.0)
citation.version_coded: Version of record (publisher layout, CC BY) from the University of Trento IRIS repository listed by OpenAlex (hdl.handle.net/11572/385392), PDF (16 pp.) read in full as text. The HAL and Queen Mary copies served bot challenges and were not used

included.reason: I-SPEED (screening code kept at full text; the only measured classical comparison is per dispersion-diagram evaluation, a cost proxy as in P00149)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: A CNN surrogate predicts a phononic unit cell's full dispersion diagram in under 100 ms, versus roughly 0.5-1 h for an FEM (COMSOL) calculation, so a genetic algorithm can use it inside the topology optimization loop.
claim.key_phrase: capable of predicting dispersion curves in less than 100 ms
claim.location: Sec. 4 Conclusions, pp. 12-13 (first quantitative classical comparison; the abstract and introduction are qualitative); supporting timing example in Sec. 2.1, p. 4 (about 47 min for one 134,040-DOF FEM run)
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Derived lower bound: 0.5 h (1,800 s) ÷ 0.1 s = 18,000 (36,000 at 1 h; 28,200 for the 47 min example [derived]); the article gives no factor. Per evaluation, not per optimization; no GA+FEM run is timed. Against the ≈288 s per sample implied by the dataset generation (about one month for 9,000 samples) [derived], the ratio would be about 2,900 [derived].
claim.alternatives: (1) Sec. 2.1, p. 4: about 47 min for 24 eigenmodes on a 14,072-element, 134,040-DOF mesh (AMD Ryzen 7 1800X, 64 GB), against under 100 ms for the surrogate. (2) Abstract, qualitative: the surrogate is ultrafast and can be used efficiently in the optimization framework. (3) Table 3, quality: surrogate-predicted gap-to-mid-gap ratios up to 48.1% and cumulative gap 134 kHz, not compared with any classical design.

baseline.classical_method: FEM computation of the dispersion diagram (Bloch-Floquet eigenvalue problem over Γ-X-M) in COMSOL Multiphysics: the forward solver a classical GA-based phononic TO would call for every candidate (Sec. 2.1, 4). No classical optimization run is timed or compared
baseline.implementation: COMSOL Multiphysics (commercial, general-purpose FE) driven by MATLAB LiveLink with GMSH meshes (Sec. 2.3)
baseline.hardware_classical: AMD Ryzen 7 1800X 8-core 3.8 GHz, 64 GB RAM for the 47 min example (Sec. 2.1); an unspecified desktop computer for the dataset (Sec. 2.3)
baseline.hardware_ml: not stated (Keras model imported into MATLAB, Sec. 3)
baseline.problem_size: 3D aluminium unit cell, 8 mm × 8 mm × 3 mm, with one through-cavity (Sec. 2.2); timing example mesh 14,072 tetrahedra, 134,040 DOFs, 24 eigenmodes (Sec. 2.1); dataset mesh size not stated; surrogate input 256×256 binary image, output 1,464 frequencies (about 24 modes) (Sec. 2.3-2.5)
baseline.classical_iterations: not applicable (one eigenvalue sweep per design). GA: 400 individuals, at most 50 generations, 40 stall generations, 21 design variables (Sec. 3)
baseline.classical_time: About 47 min for the 134,040-DOF example (Sec. 2.1); approximately 0.5-1 h per FEM calculation (Sec. 4); dataset of 9,000 samples in about one month (Sec. 2.3) [≈288 s per sample, derived]
baseline.ml_time: Under 100 ms per dispersion diagram (Sec. 2.1, 4); hardware and batch size not stated; GA run time not stated
baseline.training_time: not stated (hyperband hyperparameter search and early stopping, Sec. 2.5)
baseline.data_generation_cost: About one month on one desktop computer for 9,000 COMSOL samples (Sec. 2.3)
baseline.quality_metric: MSE (kHz²) and maximum frequency error (kHz) of surrogate dispersion diagrams against FEM (Table 2, Fig. 7); for optimized cells, surrogate-predicted objective values, BG% and band edges (Table 3) with FEM curves overlaid in Figs. 8-11 (qualitative)
baseline.quality_gap: Test MSE 9.8 (cross-like), 12.1 (diagonal-like), 8.1 (blot-like) kHz²; training 6.1, 4.5, 5.4 kHz² (Table 2); maximum error 9.1 to 15.4 kHz in three random test cases (Fig. 7); one optimized cell where the surrogate mispredicts multiple band gaps (Fig. 9, run 2)

R1.evidence: Sec. 2.3, 2.6 and 4: surrogate accuracy is reported against FEM on all 300 test samples (Table 2), so quality is reported at the level of the claim. Matching is loose. The quoted 0.5-1 h (and the 47 min example) concern FEM runs that appear finer or slower than the simplified-geometry FEM that produced the training labels: the dataset works out to ≈288 s per sample [derived]. The article itself says the cavity geometry was simplified to cut COMSOL time. No optimization-level comparison exists.

R2.evidence: Sec. 2.1, 2.3: the classical cost comes from general-purpose commercial FE (COMSOL via MATLAB LiveLink) on an 8-core CPU. The quoted per-evaluation time is 6-12× the ≈288 s implied by the authors' own dataset pipeline [derived], and the surrogate's hardware is not stated. (c) cannot be established: the example has 134,040 DOFs, but whether the surrogate ran on a GPU is not stated. (b) not observed: the abstract has no figure. (d) and (e) not applicable.

R3.evidence: Sec. 2.3: data generation is reported (about one month for 9,000 samples); training time is not, and no break-even is given. Sec. 1 notes qualitatively that the speed comes at the cost of supervised training. C3 [derived]: at ≈288 s per FEM sample, the data cost equals 9,000 FEM evaluations; at the quoted 0.5-1 h, 720-1,440 evaluations. One GA run allows up to 20,000 evaluations (400 × 50), so the data cost is repaid within about one run, training excluded.

R4.evidence: Table 2: surrogate outputs are FE-checked on every test sample. Optimized cells are re-analysed with FEM, but only as curve overlays (Figs. 8-11); the Table 3 values are surrogate predictions. Wall-thickness feasibility is discussed (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 12); one surrogate misprediction is disclosed (Fig. 9) without a rate. A stricter reading gives fail: the two runs shown per objective were picked from several GA runs, with no stated selection rule (Sec. 3.2).

reporting.n_test_cases: Surrogate: 100 test samples per cavity type, 300 in total (Sec. 2.6, Table 2). Optimization: four objective settings (F1; F4 at 150 and 200 kHz; F9), two selected GA runs each (Table 3, Figs. 8-11), plus a wall-thickness sweep of 0.2-1.4 mm for F1 (Fig. 12)

notes: Domain judgment for the verifier: the physics is elastodynamic band gaps (Lamb waves) of a solid aluminium plate with cavities, governed by the elastic wave equation (Eq. 1). This record treats it as solid-mechanics metamaterial design, in scope (the protocol's stated extension to the domain the template excluded), not as excluded acoustic TO. The screener did the same. If the verifier reads phononic band-gap design as acoustic TO, the code is FT-DOMAIN, and the same call applies to P00605 and P00893. The optimizer is a MATLAB genetic algorithm over 21 NURBS shape variables with the surrogate as fitness evaluator; the classical comparator is the per-evaluation FEM solve, as in P00149 (speed stratum by cost proxy). If the verifier rejects the proxy, no other classical comparison remains (the intro cites GA-based designs with gaps above 60% [15] but does not compare), so the next code would be FT-NOBASELINE. Physics code 'other' follows screening. Data: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.8063241 (ref [34]); no code link, so retest_candidate is false. GA runs differ between runs per the text, and no spread is given. The declaration notes that co-author W. Ostachowicz is an editorial board member of the journal. No author named Jun Wang. Screening code was I-SPEED. Adjudication (2026-09-24): the adjudicator re-read the CC BY version of record from the University of Trento IRIS repository (iris.unitn.it, handle 11572/385392; PDF 16 pp., no bot check), the route both coders used. The Conclusion (Sec. 4, p. 13) gives under 100 ms against approximately 0.5-1 h per FEM calculation, and Sec. 2.1 (p. 4) gives the 47 min example; the in-scope reading of elastic-wave design follows PROTOCOL §11 (elastic-wave clarification).

claimed_speedup.reason: The primary outcome is the Conclusion's comparison (Sec. 4, p. 13): under 100 ms against approximately 0.5-1 h per FEM calculation, i.e. 18,000-36,000 [derived], and the project enters the lower bound of a stated range (as in adjudicated record P00140). The second coder's 28,200 comes from the 47 min worked example in Sec. 2.1 (p. 4), a main-text alternative that §5.1 ranks after the Conclusion.
